subject: Archaeology
title: Rescue Archaeology: Racing Bulldozers
description: A 60-second lesson on Rescue Archaeology: Racing Bulldozers.

hook.text: Every new subway or highway means archaeologists must dig before bulldozers arrive.

buildup.text: London's Crossrail uncovered 10,000 artifacts, including a Tudor bowling green.

discovery.text: Developer-funded rescue digs are now the largest employer of archaeologists.

twist.text: Time pressure means sites are recorded in weeks that would normally take years.

climax.text: Without rescue laws, most urban sites would be destroyed without anyone knowing.

punchline.text: Every subway tunnel is a time machine. Archaeologists ride first.

quiz.question: Who typically funds rescue archaeology digs?
options: Government cultural heritage departments using taxes
Developers are required to fund excavation before building
University archaeology departments using research grants

details.summary: Rescue archaeology — also called salvage or preventive archaeology — documents sites threatened by construction, development, or natural erosion. Archaeologists work against tight deadlines to record and recover evidence before bulldozers, highways, and dams destroy it forever.
details.whyItMatters: Most archaeology done worldwide is rescue work, not planned research. Without legal requirements for pre-construction surveys, most new sites would be destroyed unrecorded.
takeaways: Rescue archaeology documents sites before construction destroys them
Most archaeological work worldwide is rescue-driven, not research-driven
Legal mandates require surveys before major construction projects

faq.question: What laws require rescue archaeology before construction?
faq.answer: In the US, Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act requires federal projects to assess impacts on historic properties. The UK's planning system requires archaeological evaluation before development. EU countries have similar laws mandating pre-construction archaeological assessment.

faq.question: How do archaeologists work under construction deadlines?
faq.answer: Teams use machine-assisted excavation for overburden removal, prioritize significant features, and maintain detailed photographic records. When time runs out, remaining deposits are sealed for future investigation. The tension between developer timelines and thorough recording is constant.
